bank.q: What does the name "Mesopotamia" mean?
bank.why: Mesopotamia means "between rivers," referring to the Tigris and Euphrates.
bank.hint: The region is defined by two famous waterways.

dw.Land of the gods: This is a sacred-sounding title, but the name Mesopotamia is a Greek description of the rivers.
dw.Cradle of healing: The lecture calls Mesopotamia the cradle of civilization, not specifically the cradle of healing.
dw.Fertile valley: The region was fertile farmland, but its name comes from its rivers, not its soil.

bank.q: Which two rivers give Mesopotamia its name?
bank.why: Mesopotamia lies "between rivers": the Tigris and the Euphrates.
bank.hint: Neither river runs through Egypt or India.

dw.Nile and Euphrates: The Nile runs through Egypt, so only the Euphrates belongs to Mesopotamia.
dw.Indus and Ganges: The Indus and Ganges are rivers of the Indian subcontinent, not Mesopotamia.
dw.Tigris and Nile: The Nile is Egyptian; Mesopotamia lies between the Tigris and the Euphrates.

bank.q: Which modern-day areas does Mesopotamia cover?
bank.a: Iraq, eastern Syria and southeastern Turkey
d: Egypt, Sudan and the northern coast of Libya
Greece, Cyprus and the western coast of Turkey
bank.why: The slides place Mesopotamia in modern-day Iraq, eastern Syria and southeastern Turkey.

dw.Egypt, Sudan and the northern coast of L: Egypt, Sudan and Libya are North African lands, not the Tigris-Euphrates region.
dw.Iran, Afghanistan and northwestern Pakis: Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan lie farther east, outside the Mesopotamian core.
dw.Greece, Cyprus and the western coast of: Greece, Cyprus and western Turkey are Mediterranean and Aegean areas, not Mesopotamia.

bank.q: Is Mesopotamia a civilization or an era?
bank.a: A geographical region where several civilizations developed
d: A single civilization founded and ruled by the Sumerians
An era of history that ended with the Old Babylonian Period
One city-state built on the banks of the Tigris River
bank.why: Mesopotamia refers primarily to a geographical region. The Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians all developed there.
bank.hint: Several peoples lived there over thousands of years.

dw.A single civilization founded and ruled: Several peoples, including Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians, also developed there, not just Sumerians.
dw.An era of history that ended with the Ol: The region continued long after the Old Babylonian Period, through Assyrian and later civilizations.
dw.One city-state built on the banks of the: Mesopotamia held many city-states, not a single city built on the Tigris.

bank.q: Which list names civilizations that developed in Mesopotamia?
bank.why: The slides list the Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians.
bank.hint: Pick the list with no Egyptians, Greeks or Romans.

dw.Sumerians, Egyptians, Persians and Greek: Egyptians, Persians and Greeks developed outside Mesopotamia; only the four listed peoples were Mesopotamian.
dw.Akkadians, Hittites, Romans and Minoans: Hittites, Romans and Minoans belonged to Anatolia, Italy and Crete, not Mesopotamia.
dw.Babylonians, Phoenicians, Mayans and Ass: Phoenicians and Mayans lived in the Levant and Mesoamerica, far from Mesopotamia.

bank.q: Which region does the lecture call the "cradle of the world's earliest civilization"?
bank.why: Mesopotamia is described as the cradle of the world's earliest civilization.

dw.Egypt: Egyptian civilization arose along the Nile, and the lecture does not call it the earliest cradle.
dw.Greece: Classical Greece appeared much later than the world's earliest civilization in Mesopotamia.
dw.China: Chinese civilization developed independently in East Asia, not in the cradle cited by the lecture.

bank.q: During which period did the earliest Mesopotamian medical practice appear?
bank.why: The earliest medical practice dates to the Uruk Period (c. 4000 to 3100 BCE).
bank.hint: It is the oldest period named in the lecture.

dw.Old Babylonian Period: The Old Babylonian Period is when medicine became an established profession, not when it began.
dw.Akkadian Period: The Akkadian Period came after Uruk and is not the earliest period with medical practice.
dw.Assyrian Period: The Assyrian Period came much later, long after the earliest medical practice.

bank.q: In which period did Mesopotamian medicine become a well-established profession, with knowledge recorded in written texts?
bank.why: By the Old Babylonian Period (c. 1894 to 1595 BCE), medicine was an established profession with written texts.

dw.Uruk Period: The Uruk Period held the earliest medical practice, before medicine became a written profession.
dw.Akkadian Period: The Akkadian Period is not the era the slides credit with established written medicine.
dw.Third Dynasty of Ur Period: The Third Dynasty of Ur was an earlier Sumerian revival, not the period of established written medicine.

bank.q: What are the approximate dates of the Uruk Period?
bank.why: Uruk Period: c. 4000 to 3100 BCE. (1894 to 1595 BCE is Old Babylonian; 3300 to 525 BCE is Egyptian medicine.)

dw.c. 1894 to 1595 BCE: These are the Old Babylonian dates, not the much earlier Uruk Period.
dw.c. 3300 to 525 BCE: These dates describe Egyptian medicine, which lasted from about 3300 to 525 BCE.
dw.c. 600 BCE to 500 CE: This range covers much later eras, not the prehistoric Uruk Period of 4000 to 3100 BCE.

bank.q: What are the approximate dates of the Old Babylonian Period?
bank.why: Old Babylonian Period: c. 1894 to 1595 BCE.
bank.hint: It falls in the second millennium BCE.

dw.c. 4000 to 3100 BCE: These are the Uruk Period dates, thousands of years before the Old Babylonian Period.
dw.c. 3300 to 525 BCE: This is the span of Egyptian medicine, not the Old Babylonian Period.
dw.c. 460 to 370 BCE: These are the dates of Hippocrates and classical Greek medicine.

bank.q: Most of what is known about Mesopotamian medicine comes from which source?
bank.why: Cuneiform tablets recorded symptoms, treatments, prescriptions and other medical knowledge.
bank.hint: The writing was pressed into clay.

dw.Medical papyri: Medical papyri are Egyptian records written on reed paper, not Mesopotamian clay tablets.
dw.The Rosetta Stone: The Rosetta Stone helped decipher Egyptian writing but is not a Mesopotamian medical source.
dw.Sanskrit Samhitas: Sanskrit Samhitas are Indian medical texts with no connection to Mesopotamia.

bank.q: In Mesopotamian spiritual medicine, illness was believed to involve what?
d: An imbalance of the four humors
bank.why: Spiritual medicine held that illness involved gods, demons or spirits.

dw.An imbalance of the four humors: The four humors are a Greek theory of illness, not part of Mesopotamian spiritual medicine.
dw.Bad air from rotting matter: Bad air from decaying matter is the later miasma theory, not the Mesopotamian spiritual view.
dw.A blocked flow of qi: Blocked qi belongs to traditional Chinese medicine, not Mesopotamian beliefs about illness.

bank.q: Which of these belongs to Mesopotamian SPIRITUAL medicine?
d: Herbal remedies, poultices and wound treatment
bank.why: Spiritual medicine used prayers, incantations, spells, amulets, astrology, divination and omens. The other options are practical medicine.

dw.Herbal remedies, poultices and wound tre: Herbal remedies, poultices and wound care are practical medicine, not ritual spiritual practice.
dw.Surgery and dentistry: Surgery and dentistry are hands-on practical treatments, not spiritual rituals.
dw.Cleanliness and physical treatments: Cleanliness and physical treatments belong to practical medicine, not the spiritual category.

bank.q: Which of these was part of Mesopotamian PRACTICAL medicine?
d: Incantations, spells and prayers to the gods
Astrology and divination by the priests
bank.why: Practical medicine included herbal remedies, medicines, wound treatment, surgery, dentistry and cleanliness.

dw.Incantations, spells and prayers to the: Incantations, spells and prayers are spiritual practices, not practical medicine.
dw.Amulets, omens and protective charms: Amulets, omens and protective charms are ritual spiritual tools, not practical treatment.
dw.Astrology and divination by the priests: Astrology and divination are spiritual practices performed by priests, not practical medicine.

bank.q: What do the slides mean by "Mesopotamian medicine was not purely magic"?
bank.a: Healers also used practical treatments like herbs, wound care and surgery
d: Mesopotamians rejected every religious explanation of illness
Magic was banned by the Old Babylonian kings in favor of surgery
Only priests were allowed to treat the sick, and only with spells
bank.why: Mesopotamian medicine combined spiritual medicine with practical medicine.
bank.hint: Two kinds of medicine existed side by side.

dw.Mesopotamians rejected every religious e: Mesopotamians kept religious explanations of illness; they did not reject them all.
dw.Magic was banned by the Old Babylonian k: No Old Babylonian ban on magic existed; spiritual and practical medicine coexisted.
dw.Only priests were allowed to treat the s: Practical healers like the Asu treated patients; healing was not limited to priests and spells.

bank.q: Mesopotamians used willow bark (and plants like myrtle) as what?
d: An anesthetic drink taken with wine before surgery
A disinfectant for cleaning surgical tools
A treatment for fever after childbirth
bank.why: Willow bark served as a natural painkiller and anti-inflammatory.

dw.An anesthetic drink taken with wine befo: Willow bark was used for pain and swelling, not as a drink to anesthetize surgery patients.
dw.A disinfectant for cleaning surgical too: It was a painkiller, not a disinfectant; cleanliness was a separate practical measure.
dw.A treatment for fever after childbirth: The lecture ties willow bark to pain and inflammation, not to fever after childbirth.

bank.q: Mesopotamian medicine had no pills. How were remedies usually applied instead?
bank.why: There were no pills; remedies were applied as poultices.

dw.As injections: Injections require syringes and needles, which did not exist in ancient Mesopotamia.
dw.As inhaled gases: Inhaled gases are a modern form of anesthesia, unknown to Mesopotamian healers.
dw.As acupuncture needles: Acupuncture needles belong to traditional Chinese medicine, not Mesopotamian practice.

bank.q: Who was the Sumerian goddess of healing and the principal deity associated with medicine?
bank.why: Gula was the Sumerian goddess of healing who guided doctors and dentists.

dw.Ninazu: Ninazu was a male god, the son of Gula, not the goddess of healing herself.
dw.Lamashtu: Lamashtu was a demon believed to cause illness, not a healing deity.
dw.Asipu: An Asipu was a religious healer, a human practitioner, not a goddess.

bank.q: Which other names does the lecture associate with Gula?
bank.why: The slides link Gula with Ninkarrak and Ninisinna.
bank.hint: Both names begin with "Nin", and neither is her son.

dw.Ninazu and Lamashtu: Ninazu is Gula's son and Lamashtu is a demon, so neither is another name for her.
dw.Asu and Asipu: Asu and Asipu are types of healers, not alternative names of the goddess Gula.
dw.Imhotep and Djoser: Imhotep and Djoser are Egyptian figures, unrelated to the Mesopotamian goddess Gula.

bank.q: Ninazu, the son of Gula, was associated with which of the following?
bank.a: Healing, serpents, transformation and the underworld
d: Agriculture, tea, farming and herbal medicine
Childbirth, fertility, pregnancy and women's health
Dreams, temples, pilgrimages and sacred sleep
bank.why: Ninazu was linked to healing, serpents, transformation and the underworld.
bank.hint: Think about the modern medical symbol.

dw.Agriculture, tea, farming and herbal med: Agriculture, tea and farming resemble the Chinese sage Shennong, not Ninazu's domains.
dw.Childbirth, fertility, pregnancy and wom: Childbirth, fertility and women's health belong to gynecological concerns, not Ninazu.
dw.Dreams, temples, pilgrimages and sacred: Dreams and sacred sleep suggest Greek incubation at temples of Asclepius, not Ninazu.

bank.q: The rod intertwined with serpents, now associated with the medical profession, is linked in the lecture source to which figure?
bank.why: The slides link the serpent rod to Ninazu, the god of healing and serpents.
bank.hint: A Mesopotamian god, son of a goddess.

dw.Gula: Gula was Ninazu's mother; the lecture links the serpent rod to her son.
dw.Imhotep: Imhotep was an Egyptian physician later deified, not the figure tied to the serpent rod.
dw.Shennong: Shennong is a Chinese legendary sage linked to herbs and farming, not the serpent rod.

bank.q: What was an Asu in Mesopotamia?
bank.a: A practical physician using herbs, physical treatments and wound care
d: A spiritual healer who used incantations, spells and divination
The goddess who guided doctors and dentists in treating illness
A demon believed to cause illness, driven away by rituals
bank.why: The Asu treated illness with practical, empirical methods.
bank.hint: The shorter name is the practical healer.

dw.A spiritual healer who used incantations: That describes the Asipu, the religious healer who used rituals and divination.
dw.The goddess who guided doctors and denti: That describes Gula, the goddess who guided doctors and dentists.
dw.A demon believed to cause illness, drive: That describes Lamashtu, a demon blamed for illness, not a physician.

bank.q: What was an Asipu in Mesopotamia?
bank.a: A religious healer using prayers, incantations, spells and divination
d: A practical physician who treated wounds with herbs, poultices and bandages
A scribe who copied prescriptions onto cuneiform tablets
A healer who set fractures and pulled teeth by hand
bank.why: The Asipu performed rituals to drive away supernatural causes of illness.

dw.A practical physician who treated wounds: That describes the Asu, the practical physician who treated wounds with herbs.
dw.A scribe who copied prescriptions onto c: Scribes copied texts but were not the ritual healers who drove away supernatural causes.
dw.A healer who set fractures and pulled te: Setting fractures and pulling teeth was practical work done by the Asu.

bank.q: A Mesopotamian family believes the demon Lamashtu is making their child sick. Which healer would they most likely call?
bank.why: The Asipu performed rituals to drive away or protect patients from supernatural causes of illness such as Lamashtu.

dw.An Asu: An Asu treated physical problems with herbs and wound care, not demon-caused illness.
dw.A Hippocratic physician: Hippocratic physicians were later Greek healers who did not practice Mesopotamian ritual medicine.
dw.A barber-surgeon: Barber-surgeons were medieval European practitioners, not ancient Mesopotamian healers.

bank.q: A Mesopotamian laborer has a deep cut on his arm. A healer cleans it and applies an herbal poultice. Which kind of healer is this?
bank.why: The Asu used practical methods such as herbal remedies and wound care.
bank.hint: The treatment is physical, not spiritual.

dw.An Asipu: An Asipu addressed supernatural causes through ritual, not a physical wound with a poultice.
dw.A diviner reading omens: A diviner read omens for spiritual diagnosis; this healer is doing hands-on treatment.
dw.A priest of Asclepius: A priest of Asclepius served a Greek healing cult, not Mesopotamian practical medicine.

bank.q: Ancient Egyptian medicine developed along the Nile during roughly which period?
bank.why: Egyptian medicine developed along the Nile from about 3300 to 525 BCE.

dw.4000 to 3100 BCE: Those are the Uruk Period dates in Mesopotamia, not the span of Egyptian medicine.
dw.1894 to 1595 BCE: That range is the Old Babylonian Period in Mesopotamia, not ancient Egyptian medicine.
dw.460 to 370 BCE: Those are the years of Hippocrates and classical Greek medicine, not Egyptian practice.

bank.q: Where did Egyptians record their knowledge of diseases, anatomy, medicines, treatments and surgery?
bank.why: Egyptians recorded medical knowledge in medical papyri.
bank.hint: Made from a reed that grows along the Nile.

dw.On cuneiform tablets: Cuneiform tablets were Mesopotamian clay records, not the papyri used in Egypt.
dw.In Sanskrit Samhitas: Sanskrit Samhitas are ancient Indian medical texts, not Egyptian records.
dw.In woodcut atlases: Woodcut atlases are Renaissance European anatomy books, far later than Egypt.

bank.q: How does the lecture describe the Egyptian healthcare system?
bank.a: It combined clinical treatment with religious and magical practices
d: It relied mainly on spells, prayers and rituals, with little hands-on care
It rejected religion entirely in favor of surgery and herbs
It was run only by foreign Greek physicians trained in Athens
bank.why: Egyptian healthcare combined clinical procedures with spells and rituals for illnesses believed to have supernatural causes.

dw.It relied mainly on spells, prayers and: Egyptian healers also used practical examination and treatment, not just spells and amulets.
dw.It rejected religion entirely in favor o: Egyptians did not reject religion; they combined it with clinical procedures.
dw.It was run only by foreign Greek physici: Greek physicians trained in Athens came later and did not run Egyptian healthcare.

bank.q: Who served as a high official under Pharaoh Djoser and became one of the most famous medical figures of ancient Egypt?
bank.why: Imhotep was a high official under Pharaoh Djoser.

dw.Asclepius: Asclepius was the Greek god of healing, not an official under Djoser.
dw.Ninazu: Ninazu was a Mesopotamian deity, the son of Gula, not an Egyptian official.
dw.Jivaka: Jivaka was a physician in ancient India, not an Egyptian serving Djoser.

bank.q: Imhotep served as a high official under which pharaoh?
bank.why: Imhotep served under Pharaoh Djoser.

dw.Ramses: Ramses was a later Egyptian pharaoh, not Imhotep's patron.
dw.Tutankhamun: Tutankhamun ruled in the 18th Dynasty, long after Imhotep's time.
dw.Khufu: Khufu built the Great Pyramid in the 4th Dynasty; Imhotep served Djoser.

bank.q: Why is the Rosetta Stone important to the history of Egyptian medicine?
bank.a: Its translation made it possible to read Egypt's medical records
d: It is the oldest Egyptian surgical textbook ever found
It lists Imhotep's prescriptions for treating fractures
It describes the first Egyptian vaccine against plague
bank.why: Translating the Rosetta Stone let scholars understand Egyptian writing and eventually interpret medical records.
bank.hint: It is a key to a language.

dw.It is the oldest Egyptian surgical textb: The oldest surgical text is the Edwin Smith Papyrus, not the Rosetta Stone.
dw.It lists Imhotep's prescriptions for tre: The Rosetta Stone is a multilingual decree; it does not list Imhotep's prescriptions.
dw.It describes the first Egyptian vaccine: Egyptians had no plague vaccine; vaccination is a much later discovery.

bank.q: In what year was the Rosetta Stone translated?
bank.why: The Rosetta Stone was translated in 1822.

dw.1816: Champollion announced the decipherment in 1822, not 1816.
dw.1851: The translation came in 1822, decades before 1851.
dw.1895: The Rosetta Stone was read in 1822, not at the end of the century.

bank.q: Which papyrus contains prescriptions and information on general medicine, diseases, medications and magical treatments?
bank.why: The Ebers Papyrus covers prescriptions, general medicine and magical treatments.

dw.Edwin Smith Papyrus: The Edwin Smith Papyrus covers injuries and surgery, not general prescriptions.
dw.Kahun Gynecological Papyrus: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus deals with women's health, not broad general medicine.
dw.London Medical Papyrus: The London Medical Papyrus is a smaller recipe collection, not the comprehensive general text.

bank.q: Which papyrus focuses on injuries, wounds, fractures, anatomy, patient examination and surgical treatment?
bank.why: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is the injury and surgery papyrus.

dw.Ebers Papyrus: The Ebers Papyrus focuses on prescriptions and general medicine, not trauma surgery.
dw.Kahun Gynecological Papyrus: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus concerns women's health, not wounds and fractures.
dw.Hearst Papyrus: The Hearst Papyrus is a collection of remedies, not a surgical trauma text.

bank.q: Which papyrus discusses women's health, fertility, pregnancy and diseases of women?
bank.why: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus deals with women's health.
bank.hint: Its full name gives it away.

dw.Ebers Papyrus: The Ebers Papyrus is a broad general medical text, not the gynecological one.
dw.Edwin Smith Papyrus: The Edwin Smith Papyrus covers trauma and surgery, not women's health.
dw.London Medical Papyrus: The London Medical Papyrus holds general recipes, not a gynecological treatise.

bank.q: A historian wants to learn how Egyptian physicians examined and treated a broken arm. Which papyrus should they read first?
bank.why: Fractures, wounds and surgical treatment are the focus of the Edwin Smith Papyrus.

dw.Kahun Gynecological Papyrus: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus deals with women's health, not broken bones.
dw.Ebers Papyrus: The Ebers Papyrus covers general medicine and prescriptions, not fracture surgery.
dw.Hearst Papyrus: The Hearst Papyrus is a remedy collection, not a surgical guide to fractures.

bank.q: A researcher studying how ancient Egyptians handled fertility problems and pregnancy would look mainly at which source?
bank.why: The Kahun Gynecological Papyrus discusses fertility, pregnancy and gynecological conditions.

dw.Edwin Smith Papyrus: The Edwin Smith Papyrus focuses on injuries and surgery, not fertility.
dw.Ebers Papyrus: The Ebers Papyrus is general medicine, not a text on pregnancy.
dw.Charaka Samhita of ancient India: The Charaka Samhita is an ancient Indian text, not an Egyptian source.

bank.q: Which of these is NOT one of the Egyptian medical papyri named in the lecture?
bank.why: The papyri named are Ebers, Edwin Smith, Kahun, Hearst and London. Charaka is the Indian author of the Charaka Samhita.

dw.Hearst Papyrus: The Hearst Papyrus is one of the Egyptian medical papyri named in the lecture.
dw.London Medical Papyrus: The London Medical Papyrus is another Egyptian medical text named in the lecture.
dw.Kahun Papyrus: The Kahun Papyrus is an Egyptian gynecological papyrus, so it belongs on the list.

bank.q: Which best describes "organized medical practice" in ancient Egypt?
bank.a: Physicians examined, diagnosed, predicted outcomes and prescribed treatment
d: Healers relied mainly on spells and amulets, with little examination of patients
Priests timed every treatment with the movement of the stars
Barbers performed all surgery in public squares for a fee
bank.why: Egyptian physicians followed an organized process from examination to prescription.
bank.hint: It sounds like a modern consultation.

dw.Healers relied mainly on spells and amul: Egyptian physicians did examine patients; spells did not replace clinical care.
dw.Priests timed every treatment with the m: Astrological timing is not the organized examination-to-prescription process described.
dw.Barbers performed all surgery in public: Barber-surgeons were medieval European practitioners, not ancient Egyptian physicians.

bank.q: Egyptian medicinal remedies were made from which ingredients?
bank.a: Herbs and plants, honey, milk, animal fat, minerals and metals
d: Mercury, sulfur and salt prepared by early chemists
Cowpox fluid and bacteria weakened in a laboratory
Cannabis, monkshood and datura mixed into wine
bank.why: Egyptians used herbs, plants, honey, milk, animal fat, minerals and metals for illnesses, wounds and skin conditions.
bank.hint: Mostly natural plant and household ingredients.

dw.Mercury, sulfur and salt prepared by ear: Mercury and sulfur remedies belong to later alchemy, not Egyptian medicine.
dw.Cowpox fluid and bacteria weakened in a: Cowpox and laboratory bacteria describe modern vaccination, not ancient Egyptian remedies.
dw.Cannabis, monkshood and datura mixed int: Monkshood and datura are dangerous plants used elsewhere, not the Egyptian remedy ingredients.

bank.q: Why did Egyptian physicians sometimes combine treatments with spells, prayers, rituals and amulets?
bank.a: Some illnesses were believed to have supernatural causes
d: The pharaoh had banned practical medicine for ordinary commoners
Spells were thought to be the only way to clean tools
Only priests were allowed to read the medical papyri
bank.why: Religious and magical practices were used for illnesses believed to have supernatural causes.
bank.hint: What did they believe caused some illnesses?

dw.The pharaoh had banned practical medicin: No pharaoh banned practical medicine; ordinary Egyptians still received treatment.
dw.Spells were thought to be the only way t: Tool cleanliness was a practical measure, not something spells alone handled.
dw.Only priests were allowed to read the me: Physicians and scribes, not only priests, read and used the medical papyri.

bank.q: According to the lecture, which areas did Egyptian physicians understand or perform?
bank.a: Anatomy, dentistry, wound care and fracture treatment
d: Blood circulation through a closed system pumped by the heart
Germ theory, pasteurization and laboratory vaccines
bank.why: Egyptians understood anatomy, diseases, dentistry and medicine preparation, and performed wound care and fracture treatment.
bank.hint: Only one option fits the ancient world.

dw.Blood circulation through a closed syste: Closed-circuit blood circulation was described by William Harvey in 1628, not ancient Egypt.
dw.Germ theory, pasteurization and laborato: Germ theory and pasteurization are modern discoveries, unknown to Egyptian physicians.
dw.Acupuncture channels and needle techniqu: Acupuncture channels belong to traditional Chinese medicine, not Egyptian practice.

bank.q: What was ancient Greece's main contribution to the direction of medicine?
bank.a: It moved medicine toward observation and natural explanations of disease
d: It replaced observation with dreams in the temples of Asclepius
It introduced chemical remedies like mercury, sulfur and iron to Greek medicine
It proved that germs, not humors, are the cause of disease
bank.why: Greece shifted medicine toward rational observation and natural explanations, and helped establish clinical documentation.

dw.It replaced observation with dreams in t: Temple dream healing was a religious practice, not Greece's move toward rational observation.
dw.It introduced chemical remedies like mer: Chemical remedies like mercury, sulfur and iron belong to Paracelsus and later iatrochemistry.
dw.It proved that germs, not humors, are th: Germ theory came in the nineteenth century with Pasteur and Koch, not ancient Greece.

bank.q: What characterized Greek medicine in the 5th century BC?
bank.a: Physicians studied symptoms and outcomes, while temple healing continued
d: Temple healing was outlawed so that only physicians could treat
Physicians relied mainly on sacred dreams and omens to choose their treatments
Medicine was based entirely on astrology and celestial charts
bank.why: Physicians increasingly studied the body and outcomes, though religious and temple healing continued.
bank.hint: Both kinds of healing existed together.

dw.Temple healing was outlawed so that only: Temple healing was not outlawed; it continued alongside physician practice in Greece.
dw.Physicians relied mainly on sacred dream: Sacred dreams and omens belonged to temple incubation, not mainstream physician practice.
dw.Medicine was based entirely on astrology: Astrology and celestial charts were not the basis of Greek clinical medicine.

bank.q: People visited sanctuaries such as Epidaurus to seek cures through sacred dreams. Which healing figure were these sanctuaries for?
bank.why: Asclepius was a major healing figure; Epidaurus was one of his sanctuaries.
bank.hint: A legendary healer, not a historical physician.

dw.Hippocrates: Hippocrates was a historical physician, not the divine figure honored at Epidaurus.
dw.Galen: Galen was a Roman-era physician who lived centuries after Epidaurus was established.
dw.Imhotep: Imhotep was an Egyptian figure later deified, not the Greek healing god of Epidaurus.

bank.q: What were the Asclepieia?
bank.a: Temples of Asclepius that became pilgrimage sites for healing
d: The 60 treatises that make up the Hippocratic Writings
Battlefield hospitals used during the Trojan War
Schools of human anatomy founded by Galen in Rome
bank.why: Temples dedicated to Asclepius were called Asclepieia.
bank.hint: The name comes from the healer.

dw.The 60 treatises that make up the Hippoc: The roughly sixty treatises are the Hippocratic Writings, not temples.
dw.Battlefield hospitals used during the Tr: The Iliad describes battlefield wound care, not permanent hospitals called Asclepieia.
dw.Schools of human anatomy founded by Gale: Galen studied anatomy in Rome; the Asclepieia were earlier Greek healing temples.

bank.q: Which statement best describes healing at Asclepius' sanctuaries?
bank.a: Divine healing and practical care coexisted
d: Prayer alone was permitted for healing; practical treatment was forbidden
The sanctuaries were used only for dissection
bank.why: Practitioners gave practical treatments at religious sites; Greek medicine did not fully separate spirituality from physical medicine.

dw.Prayer alone was permitted for healing;: Practical treatments were provided at the sanctuaries, so prayer alone was not required.
dw.Practical treatment completely replaced: Religion remained central at the sanctuaries, so practical care never replaced it.
dw.The sanctuaries were used only for disse: Dissection was not the sanctuary's purpose; they served pilgrims seeking cures.

bank.q: Which list gives the four humors?
bank.a: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
d: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and white bile
Air, water, fire and the earth element
Yin, yang, qi and the five elements
bank.why: The four humors are blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

dw.Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and white bil: White bile is not one of the four humors; black bile completes the set.
dw.Air, water, fire and the earth element: Air, water, fire and earth are the four elements, not the bodily humors.
dw.Yin, yang, qi and the five elements: Yin, yang, qi and the five elements belong to traditional Chinese medicine.

bank.q: Which humor corresponds to the sanguine temperament (cheerful, energetic, optimistic)?
bank.why: Blood = sanguine = air = cheerful, energetic, optimistic.
bank.hint: "Sanguine" comes from the Latin word for blood.

dw.Phlegm: Phlegm corresponds to the phlegmatic temperament, which is calm and deliberate.
dw.Yellow bile: Yellow bile corresponds to the choleric temperament, which is passionate and angry.
dw.Black bile: Black bile corresponds to the melancholic temperament, prone to thoughtfulness and sadness.

bank.q: Black bile corresponds to which temperament?
bank.a: Melancholic: analytical, thoughtful, prone to sadness
bank.why: Black bile = melancholic = earth.

dw.Choleric: passionate, ambitious, easily: The choleric temperament comes from yellow bile, not black bile.
dw.Phlegmatic: calm, level-headed, delibera: The phlegmatic temperament comes from phlegm, which is calm and level-headed.
dw.Sanguine: cheerful, energetic, optimisti: The sanguine temperament comes from blood, associated with cheerfulness and energy.

bank.q: A person described as passionate, ambitious and easily angered was thought to be dominated by which humor?
bank.why: Yellow bile = choleric = fire.

That diseases come from external agents

The four humors of the body

dw.Shennong Bencao Jing: That is a Chinese herbal text, unrelated to Harvey.

dw.The authority of Galen: Harvey questioned Galen and tested ideas instead of trusting authority.

dw.Animal-only dissection: Animal dissection was Galen's method; Renaissance teaching increasingly used human bodies.
dw.Memorizing Galen word for word: Renaissance anatomists began to challenge Galen through direct observation instead of memorizing him.
dw.Astrological charts: Astrology was tied to treatment timing, not to the anatomical education of the Renaissance.

dw.1514: 1514 is Vesalius' birth year, not the publication year of the Fabrica.
dw.1590: 1590 is nearly fifty years after the Fabrica appeared in 1543.

Notes on the Human Body and Its Hospitals
The Inner Canon of the Human Body

bank.q: What kind of pictures did the Fabrica include?

Translations of ancient Egyptian medical papyri
Copies of Leonardo da Vinci's paintings

bank.q: What did Book 2 of the Fabrica cover?

bank.why: Book 3 = veins and arteries.

dw.Heart and associated structures: The heart and associated structures are covered in Book 6.

bank.q: What did Book 4 of the Fabrica cover?

bank.hint: Comes just after the blood vessels.

dw.Brain: The brain is the subject of Book 7.
dw.Bones and cartilage: Bones and cartilage begin the Fabrica in Book 1.
dw.Veins and arteries: Veins and arteries belong to Book 3.

dw.Book 6: Book 6 covers the heart and associated structures.
dw.Book 7: Book 7 covers the brain, the last topic.

bank.q: Which book of the Fabrica covered the heart and associated structures?
bank.why: Book 6 = heart and associated structures.

dw.Book 5: Book 5 covers abdominal and reproductive organs.

bank.q: Why did Renaissance artists study anatomy?
bank.a: To depict the human body more accurately
d: To qualify as barber-surgeons and earn more money
To test Paracelsus' new chemical remedies
To earn posts as royal surgeons to the king
bank.why: Artists studied anatomy to depict the body more accurately.

dw.To qualify as barber-surgeons and earn m: Barber-surgeons trained by apprenticeship for surgery and grooming, not through artists' anatomy study.
dw.To test Paracelsus' new chemical remedie: Paracelsus' chemical remedies concerned pharmacy and medicine, not artists' anatomical work.
dw.To earn posts as royal surgeons to the k: Royal surgeon posts were medical appointments, not the reason artists studied anatomy.

bank.q: What was the purpose of Leonardo da Vinci's detailed anatomical drawings?
bank.a: To show inner structures not visible from the outside
d: To decorate the walls of church hospitals
To record astrological timing for bloodletting
To illustrate Galen's studies of animals
bank.why: Leonardo's drawings revealed internal structures.

dw.To decorate the walls of church hospital: Leonardo's anatomical sheets were private study drawings, not decoration for church hospitals.
dw.To record astrological timing for bloodl: Astrological timing for bloodletting was unrelated to Leonardo's anatomical investigations.
dw.To illustrate Galen's studies of animals: Leonardo dissected humans himself rather than illustrating Galen's animal studies.

bank.q: How did anatomical drawings help Renaissance medicine?
bank.a: They allowed precise, widespread transfer of knowledge
d: They were used to time treatments by the stars
bank.why: Anatomical drawings allowed precise, widespread knowledge transfer.

dw.They replaced dissection completely: Drawings spread knowledge but did not replace hands-on dissection completely.
dw.They proved germ theory: Germ theory emerged in the nineteenth century from Pasteur and Koch.
dw.They were used to time treatments by the: Astrology governed treatment timing, not the purpose of anatomical drawings.

bank.q: According to the lecture, accurate anatomical knowledge was the first step toward what?
bank.why: The new, accurate anatomy was the first step toward effective surgery and diagnosis.
bank.hint: You must know the body before operating on it.

dw.The discovery of microscopic germs: Microscopic germs were revealed by later microscopists, not by Renaissance anatomy.
dw.Better astrological charts: Astrological charts were part of astrology and not the goal of accurate anatomy.
dw.Closing all religious hospitals: Closing religious hospitals was a later political change unrelated to anatomy.

bank.q: How does the lecture describe dissection during the Renaissance?
bank.a: A public and private tool for discovery
d: A forbidden practice done only in secret
A religious ritual for the dead
bank.why: Dissection was a public and private tool for discovery.

dw.A forbidden practice done only in secret: Renaissance dissections were held publicly as well as privately, so they were not only secret.
dw.A religious ritual for the dead: Dissection was an anatomical technique, not a religious ritual for the dead.
dw.A punishment for criminals only: Criminals were sometimes dissected, but the practice was not limited to punishment.

bank.q: What did barber-surgeons do?
bank.why: Barber-surgeons performed bloodletting and minor surgery.

dw.Major heart and brain surgery: Major heart and brain surgery was far beyond their training; they did minor procedures.
dw.Managing Church-run hospitals: Church-run hospitals were managed by religious orders, not by barber-surgeons.
dw.Writing anatomy textbooks: Anatomy textbooks were written by scholarly anatomists such as Vesalius, not barber-surgeons.

bank.q: What were leeches used for in Renaissance medicine?
bank.why: Leeches were used for bloodletting.

dw.Cleaning wounds of pus: Leeches drew blood; cleaning pus from wounds was not their purpose.
dw.Anesthesia: Anesthesia was not available in the Renaissance, and leeches do not numb pain.
dw.Closing arteries: Closing arteries was done by ligature or cauterization, not by leeches.

bank.q: What is cauterization?
bank.a: Burning tissue with heat to control bleeding
d: Tying blood vessels shut with thread
Washing wounds with a soothing balm
Removing excess blood with leeches placed on the skin
bank.why: Cauterization burns tissue with heat; it was used on wounds and after amputations.

dw.Tying blood vessels shut with thread: Tying blood vessels with thread describes a ligature, which controls bleeding without heat.
dw.Washing wounds with a soothing balm: Washing a wound with balm is wound care, not the burning used in cauterization.
dw.Removing excess blood with leeches place: Using leeches to remove blood is bloodletting, not cauterization.

bank.q: What is a ligature?
bank.a: Tying a blood vessel shut without burning
d: Burning tissue with a red-hot iron
Draining blood using leeches on the skin
Pouring boiling oil on the wound
bank.why: A ligature ties the vessel and controls bleeding without burning.

dw.Burning tissue with a red-hot iron: Burning tissue with a red-hot iron is cauterization, the method the ligature replaced.
dw.Draining blood using leeches on the skin: Draining blood with leeches is bloodletting, which does not tie off a vessel.
dw.Pouring boiling oil on the wound: Pouring boiling oil on a wound was a harsh wound treatment, not a way to tie a vessel.

bank.q: What was the main drawback of cauterization?
d: It took several weeks to work
It spread germs through the air
bank.why: Cauterization was painful and damaged tissue; the ligature avoided burning.

dw.It took several weeks to work: Cauterization acted immediately; the problem was pain and tissue damage, not delay.
dw.It required a microscope: Cauterization needed only a hot iron; microscopes were not part of the procedure.
dw.It spread germs through the air: Germ theory was not yet known, and the recorded drawback was pain and tissue damage.

bank.q: After an amputation, a surgeon ties off the arteries with thread instead of pressing a hot iron to the stump. Which method is this?

dw.Cauterization: Cauterization uses heat to burn tissue, while this case uses thread without burning.
dw.Bloodletting: Bloodletting removes blood and does not close off an artery.
dw.Emergentism: Emergentism is a drug theory about mixtures, not a method for closing an artery.

bank.q: A surgeon presses a red-hot iron against a bleeding wound to stop the bleeding. Which practice is this?
bank.why: Using heat to burn tissue and control bleeding is cauterization.

dw.Ligature: A ligature ties the vessel with thread and involves no heat.
dw.Prosthetics: Prosthetics replaces missing body parts and does not stop bleeding.
dw.Pasteurization: Pasteurization heats liquids to kill microbes; it is not a wound treatment.

bank.q: Which was an impact of Renaissance surgery?
bank.a: Surgery became more observation-based, with better bleeding control
d: Infection rates dropped to almost zero after surgery
Anesthesia made major operations painless for the first time in Europe
Germ theory began to guide every operation

dw.Anesthesia made major operations painles: Anesthesia came in the nineteenth century, not the Renaissance.
dw.Germ theory began to guide every operati: Germ theory arose in the nineteenth century and did not guide Renaissance operations.

bank.q: Which were limitations of Renaissance surgery?

d: Too few anatomical drawings and no printing
A complete ban on human dissection
bank.why: Limitations: poor sanitation, high infection risk and high mortality.

dw.A complete ban on human dissection: Human dissection became more common in the Renaissance, not banned.

The first removal of an eye for cancer
The first tracheotomy of the windpipe

dw.The first removal of an eye for cancer: The first eye removal for cancer was done by Georg Bartisch.
dw.The first tracheotomy of the windpipe: The first tracheotomy is credited to Antonio Branca, or Brassavola.

bank.q: Which is part of the RENAISSANCE approach rather than the earlier approach?

dw.Detailed anatomical drawings: Detailed anatomical drawings were a Renaissance development, not part of the earlier approach.

bank.why: Limited illustrations gave way to detailed anatomical drawings.

dw.Anatomical photographs: Photography came later; the Renaissance replacement was hand-drawn anatomical illustration.

dw.Astrological charts: Astrological charts were not anatomical illustrations and did not replace them.

bank.q: In Renaissance drug theory, what is reductionism?
bank.a: Explaining drugs by hot, cold, wet and dry
d: Believing that drug powers come from the stars

bank.q: In reductionism, what are secondary potencies?
bank.a: General effects such as hardening and softening
d: Specific actions such as dissolving gallstones
Powers that come from the planets
bank.why: Secondary potencies are general effects (hardening, softening).

dw.Powers that come from the planets: Powers from the planets belong to celestial causation, not the potency scheme.
dw.New effects created by mixing: New effects from mixing describe emergentism, not secondary potencies.

bank.q: In reductionism, what are tertiary potencies?
bank.a: Specific actions, such as dissolving gallstones
d: General effects, such as hardening and softening
The basic hot, cold, wet and dry qualities
Powers that flow from the heavenly bodies
bank.why: Tertiary potencies are specific actions.

dw.General effects, such as hardening and s: Hardening and softening are general secondary potencies, not tertiary ones.
dw.The basic hot, cold, wet and dry qualiti: The basic hot, cold, wet and dry qualities are primary, not tertiary potencies.
dw.Powers that flow from the heavenly bodie: Influence from heavenly bodies is celestial causation, not a tertiary potency.

bank.q: What is celestial causation?
bank.a: The belief that drug powers come from the stars
d: The belief that mixtures produce new effects
The belief that the dose makes the poison
The belief that bad air causes disease
bank.why: Celestial causation held that drug powers came from the stars and heavenly bodies.

dw.The belief that the dose makes the poiso: The dose-makes-the-poison idea is Paracelsus' toxicology principle.
dw.The belief that bad air causes disease: Bad air causing disease is miasma theory, unrelated to celestial causation.

bank.q: What is emergentism?
bank.a: The idea that mixtures have effects no single ingredient has
d: The idea that drug powers come from the stars
The idea that drugs act through hot, cold, wet and dry
The idea that diseases emerge from bad air
bank.why: Emergentism: the mixture has effects its ingredients lack alone.

dw.The idea that drug powers come from the: Drug powers from the stars define celestial causation, not emergentism.
dw.The idea that drugs act through hot, col: Acting through hot, cold, wet and dry is reductionism.
dw.The idea that diseases emerge from bad a: Disease from bad air is miasma theory, not emergentism.

dw.Celestial causation: Celestial causation attributes effects to stars, not to combining herbs.
dw.Miasma theory: Miasma theory explains disease from bad air, not from herb mixtures.

dw.Reductionism: Reductionism uses hot, cold, wet and dry qualities, not planets.
dw.Arcana: Arcana are targeted drugs, not powers drawn from planet alignment.

Drug powers come from the stars
Drugs must balance the four humors

dw.Drug powers come from the stars: Star-derived drug powers belong to celestial causation, not Arcana.
dw.Drugs must balance the four humors: Balancing the four humors is Galenic humoralism, not Arcana.

bank.q: In Paracelsus' three principles of matter, what does Sulphur represent?

dw.Toxicity: Toxicity is not one of Paracelsus' three principles of matter.

bank.q: In Paracelsus' three principles of matter, what does Mercury represent?

dw.Liquidity and volatility: Liquidity and volatility are Mercury's qualities, not those of Salt.
dw.Softness: Softness is not Salt's principle; Salt represents stability and solidity.

dw.Boiling oil: Boiling oil was Ambroise Paré's wound treatment, not Paracelsus' ointment.

items.q: Which Mesopotamian deity was the principal goddess of healing?
items.why: Gula was associated with healing and also identified as Ninkarrak and Ninisinna.

items.q: Which Mesopotamian healer used practical treatments and wound care?
items.why: The Asu was the practical physician, while the Asipu was a spiritual healer.

items.q: Which practitioner used spells, prayers, incantations and divination?
items.why: The Asipu performed rituals against supernatural causes of illness.

items.q: Which deity was linked to serpents, healing and the underworld?
items.why: Ninazu was associated with serpents, transformation, healing and the underworld.

items.q: What recorded Mesopotamian symptoms, treatments and prescriptions?
items.why: Cuneiform tablets are major sources of Mesopotamian medical knowledge.

items.q: Which papyrus primarily focused on surgery, wounds and fractures?
items.why: Edwin Smith focuses on injuries, anatomy, patient examination and surgical treatment.

items.q: Which Egyptian papyrus includes general medicine and prescriptions?
items.why: Ebers includes diseases, medicines, prescriptions and magical treatments.

items.q: Which papyrus focuses on fertility, pregnancy and women's health?
items.why: Kahun focuses on gynecological conditions and women's health.

items.q: Who served under Pharaoh Djoser and became a famous Egyptian medical figure?
items.why: Imhotep was a high official under Djoser.

items.q: Who is known as the Father of Medicine?
items.why: Hippocrates emphasized natural causes, prognosis, observation and ethics.

items.q: Who was a Greek physician during the Roman period whose writings influenced medicine for over 1,000 years?
items.why: Galen developed anatomy and physiology and expanded Hippocratic ideas.

items.q: Which legendary Greek figure was associated with healing temples at Epidaurus?
items.why: Asclepius was associated with the Asclepieia healing sanctuaries.

items.q: Which humor corresponds to sanguine temperament?
items.why: Blood is associated with air, cheerfulness and optimism.

items.q: Which humor corresponds to melancholic temperament?
items.why: Black bile is associated with earth and sadness.

items.q: Which humor corresponds to choleric temperament?
items.why: Yellow bile corresponds to fire, ambition and anger.

items.q: Which humor corresponds to phlegmatic temperament?
items.why: Phlegm corresponds to water and calmness.

items.q: Who was the Father of Indian Medicine or Ayurveda?
items.why: Charaka is associated with internal medicine and the Charaka Samhita.

items.q: Who was the Father of Surgery and Plastic Surgery?
items.why: Sushruta was associated with surgical practice and the Sushruta Samhita.

items.q: Which Sanskrit medical text focuses on internal medicine?
items.why: Charaka Samhita emphasizes Kaya Chikitsa, or internal medicine.

items.q: Which Sanskrit text focuses on surgery and anatomy?
items.why: Sushruta Samhita focuses on Shalya Tantra, or surgery.

items.q: Who was the personal physician of Gautama Buddha?
items.why: Jivaka served Buddha, King Bimbisara and the early Sangha.

items.q: What is the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon?
items.why: Huangdi Neijing is a foundational Traditional Chinese Medicine text.

items.q: Which part of the Huangdi Neijing contains Basic Questions?
items.why: Suwen focuses on theories, philosophy, illness causes and diagnosis.

items.q: Which part of the Huangdi Neijing covers acupuncture channels?
items.why: Lingshu, the Spiritual Pivot, focuses on anatomy and acupuncture.

items.q: Who was associated with the herbal anesthetic Mafeisan?
items.why: Hua Tuo is linked to Mafeisan, administered orally with wine.

items.q: Which five-element organ belongs to Wood under Yin?
items.why: Wood is associated with the liver, gallbladder and anger.

items.q: Which five-element organ belongs to Water under Yin?
items.why: Water is associated with kidneys, bladder and fear.

items.q: Who was the Father of Modern Anatomy?
items.why: Vesalius performed human dissections and corrected Galen's errors.

items.q: Who was the Father of Modern Surgery?
items.why: Pare improved wound treatment, used ligatures and developed prosthetics.

items.q: Who was the Father of Physiology in the presentation?
items.why: Harvey demonstrated blood circulation and published De Motu Cordis.

items.q: Who was the Father of Toxicology?
items.why: Paracelsus advanced chemical medicine and dose-dependent toxicity.

items.q: Who published De Humani Corporis Fabrica in 1543?
items.why: Vesalius' illustrated anatomy was based on direct dissection.

items.q: Who published De Motu Cordis?
items.why: Harvey's work supported blood circulation through experiments and mathematics.

items.q: Who demonstrated that the heart pumps blood in a closed circulatory system?
items.why: Harvey's circulation findings challenged Galen's concept of blood production.

items.q: What replaced cauterization with hot iron for controlling bleeding?
items.why: Ligatures tie arteries or blood vessels without burning tissue.

items.q: Who introduced ligatures in surgical practice?
items.why: Pare used ligatures and soothing wound treatments.

items.q: Who combined art, detailed anatomical drawings and dissections?
items.why: Leonardo studied bones, muscles, organs, embryology and the nervous system.

items.q: Which book of Fabrica concerns the brain?
items.why: Book 7 covers the brain.

items.q: Which book of Fabrica concerns veins and arteries?
items.why: Book 3 covers veins and arteries.

items.q: What is Paracelsus' principle about dosage?
items.why: Toxicity depends on how much of a substance is taken.

items.q: What does sulphur represent in Paracelsus' theory of matter?
items.why: Sulphur represents combustibility.

items.q: What does mercury represent in Paracelsus' theory of matter?
items.why: Mercury represents liquidity and volatility.

items.q: What does salt represent in Paracelsus' theory of matter?
items.why: Salt represents stability.

items.q: Which surgeon pioneered nasal reconstruction with a skin graft?
items.why: Tagliacozzi pioneered early plastic surgery techniques.

items.q: Which surgeon was associated with the first splenectomy in the slides?
items.why: Zaccarelli was listed for the first splenectomy.

items.q: Who was associated with the first eye removal for cancer?
items.why: Bartisch was listed for eye removal in cancer.

items.q: Which theoretical view held that combining ingredients produces novel effects?
items.why: Emergentism concerned effects produced by combinations of ingredients.

items.q: Who was the Father of Modern Epidemiology?
items.why: Snow investigated cholera transmission through water.

items.q: Who published an important sanitation report in 1842?
items.why: Chadwick connected poverty, filth and disease through sanitary studies.

items.q: Which theory attributed disease to bad air and rotting matter?
items.why: Miasma Theory proposed poisonous air as the cause of epidemics.

items.q: Who mapped cholera cases near the Broad Street pump?
items.why: Snow identified an association between cases and contaminated water.

items.q: Who performed the swan-neck flask experiment?
items.why: Pasteur challenged spontaneous generation in 1861.

items.q: Who formulated the four postulates establishing links between pathogens and disease?
items.why: Koch's Postulates provided an experimental framework.

items.q: Who identified the organism responsible for tuberculosis in 1882?
items.why: Koch identified the tuberculosis pathogen.

items.q: Who introduced chlorinated lime handwashing in 1847?
items.why: Semmelweis reduced puerperal fever through hand and instrument cleaning.

items.q: Who introduced carbolic acid in antiseptic surgery?
items.why: Lister used carbolic acid to disinfect wounds and instruments.

items.q: Who established the Environmental Theory of Nursing?
items.why: Nightingale emphasized ventilation, clean water, drainage, cleanliness and light.

items.q: Who pioneered Rose or Coxcomb charts for health statistics?
items.why: Nightingale used visual statistics to communicate mortality.

items.q: Who identified the anesthetic properties of nitrous oxide?
items.why: Davy observed its pain-relieving effects.

items.q: Who first used ether anesthesia clinically in 1842, according to the slides?
items.why: Long performed an operation using diethyl ether.

items.q: Who used nitrous oxide for dental extraction in 1844?
items.why: Wells used laughing gas for dental anesthesia.

items.q: Who publicly demonstrated ether anesthesia in Boston in 1846?
items.why: Morton demonstrated inhaled ether anesthesia.

items.q: Who developed smallpox vaccination based on cowpox observations?
items.why: Jenner connected cowpox exposure with protection against smallpox.

items.q: Who developed laboratory vaccines for anthrax and rabies?
items.why: Pasteur developed weakened-pathogen vaccines.

items.q: Who discovered antitoxins and serum therapy around 1890?
items.why: Von Behring developed antitoxin serum therapy for diphtheria.

items.q: Who pioneered human-to-human blood transfusion?
items.why: Blundell developed transfusion methods and instruments.

items.q: Who invented the stethoscope in 1816?
items.why: Laennec developed the early hollow-tube stethoscope.

items.q: Who invented the ophthalmoscope in 1851?
items.why: Helmholtz enabled direct examination of the retina.

items.q: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
items.why: Roentgen produced an X-ray image of his wife's hand.

items.q: Which cholera wave included John Snow's investigation in 1854?
items.why: The third wave lasted from 1846 to 1860 in the presentation.
